04 · Trends and what they mean (Task 2, interpretation)¶

Purpose: turn the scores into findings a stakeholder can act on, with the uncertainty stated.
Decisions implemented: D2 (within-type comparison, sensitivity to Stage 0 labels), D8.
Inputs → outputs: outputs/analysis/sentiment/findings.json (written by src/ti/analysis/sentiment.py), calls_table.csv, figures → findings H1 to H5.

Run from the project root or from notebooks/; nothing is written, and no model is called (replay mode).

replay mode: no network, no API key, no spend

Every number below comes from findings.json, which ti.analysis.sentiment.run() writes (percentile bootstrap over calls, 10,000 resamples; two-sided permutation tests; about 25 comparisons with no multiple-comparison correction). The cell below re-runs the analysis in memory and checks it reproduces the stored file, so nothing here is a pasted number.

In [2]:
from ti.analysis import sentiment as S
df = S.build_calls(); pt = S.build_turns(df)
f = nb.read_json("outputs/analysis/sentiment/findings.json")
chk = S.pairwise(df, "type")["support_minus_external"]["diff"]
assert abs(chk - f["q1_pairwise"]["support_minus_external"]["diff"]) < 1e-9
assert abs(S.dip_decomposition(df)["all_calls"]["diff"] - f["q2_dip"]["all_calls"]["diff"]) < 1e-9
nb.md("Re-computed support minus external and the March dip: identical to the stored findings.")

Re-computed support minus external and the March dip: identical to the stored findings.

H1 (strongest): support is the least positive call type, and the customer carries the negativity¶

In [3]:
q = f["q1_by_type"]; pw = f["q1_pairwise"]; pwt = f["q1_pairwise_title_rule"]
rows = [{"call type": t, "calls": q[t]["call_score"]["n"], "mean whole-call score": q[t]["call_score"]["mean"],
         "95% CI": str(q[t]["call_score"]["ci95"]), "mean customer-side": q[t]["customer_score"]["mean"] if q[t]["customer_score"]["n"] else None} for t in nb.TYPES]
nb.table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
nb.table(pd.DataFrame([{"comparison": k, "difference": v["diff"], "95% CI": str(v["ci95"]), "p": v["perm_p"],
                        "difference under title-rule labels": pwt[k]["diff"], "p (title rule)": pwt[k]["perm_p"]} for k, v in pw.items()]))
g = f["q1_side_gap_model_labels"]["support"]

      f"(gap {g['gap_mean']:.2f}, CI {g['gap_ci95']}); the customer is more negative in {g['calls_customer_more_negative']} of {g['n_calls']} calls.")

In support calls, 35.4% of customer turns are negative against 2.1% of staff turns (gap 0.33, CI [0.236, 0.429]); the customer is more negative in 22 of 30 calls.

What it means / who cares. The support lead should track the customer-side score, not the call average, and compare each call type only with its own baseline. Support-vs-external holds up even under the title-rule labels, so the three relabelled escalation calls do not drive it; support-vs-internal and external-vs-internal are fragile. Could be wrong if: support calls exist because something went wrong, so the gap partly reflects what the call is for, not how well it was handled.

H2: the March dip sits in the outage-touching calls¶

In [4]:
mo = f["q2_trend"]["monthly_overall"]; dip = f["q2_dip"]
nb.table(pd.DataFrame([{"month": k, "calls": v["n"], "mean": v["mean"], "95% CI": str(v["ci95"])} for k, v in mo.items()]))
nb.table(pd.DataFrame([{"version": k, "March calls": v["n_march"], "March minus other months": v["diff"], "95% CI": str(v["ci95"]), "p": v["perm_p"], "verdict": v["verdict"]}
                       for k, v in dip.items() if isinstance(v, dict) and "diff" in v and "n_march" in v]))

      f"{nb.pct(dip['touch_share_by_month']['2026-03'], 0)} of March calls are flagged.")

version March calls March minus other months 95% CI p verdict

Within March, calls that touch the outage average 2.565 (n=23) against 3.615 (n=13) for the rest; 64% of March calls are flagged.

What it means / who cares. Engineering and support leadership: the outage explains most of the dip, and it appears as a tone drop in all three call types, not just support. Removing the outage calls shrinks the dip to a size whose interval includes zero, so the data says "mostly the outage" but cannot rule out other causes (13 March calls remain). Could be wrong if: the outage flag is an LLM judgment, partly definitional; in the candidate's 20-call check it missed 3 and never over-flagged, so 42 is probably a floor (a call about an outage is tense).

H3: the outage runs through all three call types; recovery differs by account¶

In [5]:
o = f["q3_outage"]
nb.md(f"{o['n_touch']} calls touch the outage: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in o["touch_by_type"].items()) +
      f". First core-incident call: {o['first_core_incident_call']}; last: {o['last_core_incident_call']}.")
nb.table(pd.DataFrame([{"external calls": k, "n": v["n"], "mean whole-call score": v["mean"], "95% CI": str(v["ci95"])} for k, v in o["external_by_window"].items()]))
acc = []
for a in o["most_affected_accounts"]:
    cs = [x["customer_score"] for x in a["calls"] if x["customer_score"] is not None]
    acc.append({"account": a["account"] if "account" in a else a.get("org"), "calls": len(a["calls"]),
                "first customer score": cs[0] if cs else None, "last customer score": cs[-1] if cs else None})
nb.table(pd.DataFrame(acc))

What it means / who cares. Sales managers: accounts whose customer score ended lower than it started, and accounts with no call after mid-March, belong on a follow-up list. Could be wrong if: each account has only 2 to 4 calls with different purposes, so these are leads, not conclusions. Data caveat: call dates are partly inconsistent with content (a March 9 call already discusses the outage in the past tense), so we use March 10, the first outage-core call, as the boundary and avoid per-account before/after statistics.

What it means / who cares. The support lead should use trajectory as an exception report (calls that end strained), not an average. In support the share of negative turns barely falls while the score rises, which points to the scripted shape of the calls and the rubric's "relief after a fix" rule, not to proven satisfaction.

H5: we track the provided score, but measure tone where it measures severity¶

What it means / who cares. An analytics owner should report both scores and never mix them in one trend. On the war-room and remediation calls ours looks right (calm, productive); on three calls we cannot tell. Could be wrong if: there are no gold labels; ours is also an LLM judgment with design choices (courtesy neutral, lower tie-break).

What I would not claim¶

  • That sentiment predicts churn or any outcome (there are no outcome labels).
  • That internal differs from the other call types (fragile under the title-rule labels).
  • That the outage caused the dip (the flag is an LLM judgment, partly definitional; in the candidate's 20-call check it missed 3 and never over-flagged, so 42 is probably a floor).
  • Anything about trajectory as customer satisfaction.
  • Conclusions about one account from two to four calls.
  • Any statistical certainty: about 25 comparisons were made without correction, on 100 calls that appear synthetic.
